config.title: Session Timeout Hook

intro.title: Session Timeout Hook
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom React hook called `useSessionTimeout` that automatically logs a user out after a period of inactivity. You will learn the core concept of managing side effects and state over time using React hooks like `useState`, `useEffect`, and `useRef`. The main technologies involved are React with TypeScript, focusing on event listeners, timers, and cleanup functions. By the end, you'll have a reusable hook that enhances application security by handling session expiration.
intro.usecase: Session timeout hooks are essential for security and user experience in applications that handle sensitive data. In banking dashboards, they automatically log users out after periods of inactivity to prevent unauthorized access to financial information. E-commerce admin panels use them to protect order management systems while preserving unsaved work with warning modals. Healthcare portals implement these hooks to comply with HIPAA regulations by securing patient records during idle time. Developers add this pattern to any authenticated application where session security matters.

objectives: Implement a custom React hook that tracks user inactivity
Configure timeout duration and callback functions for session expiration
Initialize event listeners for user interaction detection
Manipulate timer state to reset on user activity
Apply the session timeout hook within a React component
Control the display of timeout warnings based on hook state
Integrate cleanup mechanisms to remove event listeners

steps.instruction: Create a function called useSessionTimeout that takes a parameter named timeoutInSeconds (type: number) and returns the SessionTimeoutReturn interface you defined earlier.
steps.hint: Start with either 'function useSessionTimeout(timeoutInSeconds: number): SessionTimeoutReturn' or 'const useSessionTimeout = (timeoutInSeconds: number): SessionTimeoutReturn =>'.

steps.instruction: Inside the useSessionTimeout hook function, use useState to create two state variables: timeLeft (number) and isActive (boolean). Initialize timeLeft with 0 and isActive with false.
steps.hint: Remember to import useState if you haven't already. Use destructuring to create the state variables with proper TypeScript types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The hook now has timeLeft and isActive state variables initialized with proper TypeScript types.
successCriteria: timeLeft state is declared as a number initialized to 0, and isActive state is declared as a boolean initialized to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing or incorrect. Use useState to create both timeLeft and isActive with proper types and initial values.

steps.title: Create a ref to store the interval ID
steps.instruction: Inside the useSessionTimeout hook, declare a ref using useRef to store the interval ID. Use TypeScript to type the ref as React.MutableRefObject<NodeJS.Timeout | null>.
steps.hint: Call useRef with an initial value of null and specify the type parameter to ensure TypeScript knows it holds a NodeJS.Timeout or null.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a ref for a timer ID
const timerRef = useRef<NodeJS.Timeout | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The hook now includes a ref that will persist the interval ID across renders, typed correctly for TypeScript.
successCriteria: A ref named intervalRef (or similar) is declared with useRef, typed as React.MutableRefObject<NodeJS.Timeout | null>, and initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a ref, but check the type annotation. It should be React.MutableRefObject<NodeJS.Timeout | null> to match the interval ID type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ref is missing or incorrectly typed. Use useRef with the correct TypeScript type to store the interval ID.

steps.title: Define the startTimer function
steps.instruction: Inside the useSessionTimeout hook, define a function named startTimer that sets up an interval to decrement the timeLeft state by 1 every second.
steps.hint: Use setInterval to run a callback every 1000 milliseconds. Inside the callback, update timeLeft using its setter function.
steps.expectedOutcome: A startTimer function is defined within the hook, ready to be called to begin the countdown.
successCriteria: The startTimer function is defined and uses setInterval to decrement timeLeft every second.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining startTimer, but make sure it uses setInterval to update timeLeft every 1000 milliseconds.
steps.feedbackWrong: The startTimer function is not defined or doesn't set up an interval to decrement timeLeft.

steps.hint: useCallback returns a memoized version of the callback that only changes if one of its dependencies has changed.
steps.expectedOutcome: The resetTimeout function is now memoized with useCallback, which will help prevent unnecessary re-renders in components that use this hook.
successCriteria: resetTimeout is wrapped with useCallback and has an appropriate dependency array (likely empty for this function).

steps.title: Set up useEffect to manage timer lifecycle
steps.instruction: Inside the useSessionTimeout hook, create a useEffect hook that starts the timer when the component mounts and cleans up the interval when the component unmounts.
steps.hint: Use useEffect with an empty dependency array for mount/unmount behavior. Inside, call startTimer and return a cleanup function that clears the interval using the intervalRef.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook is added to manage the timer's lifecycle, ensuring proper cleanup.
successCriteria: The useEffect hook is defined with an empty dependency array, calls startTimer, and returns a cleanup function that clears the interval using intervalRef.current.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
